genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: one of the two scientists studies the water that lies beneath the ground
the other scientist follows the watercourses in the open air
both women study the same resource
groundwater cleans itself as it passes through permeable material
surface water carries silt and plant debris along with it
surface water has to be left to settle before it can be tested
the underground store feeds the watercourse when levels are low
spells of strong flow refill the underground store
text: One of them spends half her working life underground, lamp strapped to her forehead, notebook soaking in her pocket. The other keeps to the open air, boots planted in the current, watching the rivers run. Both women measure the same water, yet they never meet it in the same condition. Beneath the rock it threads through porous ground and clears itself as it works down through beds of sand. Out in the daylight it drags along silt, fallen leaves and drowned insects, so a sample has to stand and settle before anyone can test it. The first judges a hidden reserve by how slowly it moves, the second judges a stream by its force. Set their readings side by side and a pattern shows. The buried store feeds the visible channel when levels drop, and the visible channel refills the store once the floods have passed.

units: the visitor did not expect to enjoy the visit
a first section shows what sand does when air drives it
a face of rock crumbles in front of the public behind a glass screen
a second section shows what cold does to water that has seeped in
the rock splits when water freezes inside a crack
a third section deals with chemical attack by plants
two neighbouring pebbles compare an untouched surface with a hollowed one
the fourth section is judged disappointing because of too much written matter
a model of a coastal face closes the visit
text: Honestly, I walked into the exhibition on wearing stone expecting nothing at all, and it floored me. The first room belongs to the wind. Sand is fired at a soft face of rock and the face crumbles while you watch, safe behind glass. The second room is the cold one. Water seeps into a crack, sets hard, swells, and the rock splits open like a shell. The third was my favourite, all chemistry: quiet mosses eat into limestone, and two pebbles sit side by side to prove it, one smooth, the other bitten full of hollows. The fourth room is the weak link. Too much reading, too few objects, and you switch off fast. The ending saves it, with a model cliff the water gnaws at in front of you, over and over. I came away thinking that nothing hard stays hard, and went back the same evening.

units: the writer is writing from a shelter set up beside a pool
the spring stopped flowing with no warning sign

a metal guard will be fitted upstream
text: I am writing to you from the hut down by the pool, with the ink half frozen in the pen. Yesterday at first light the spring stopped flowing, no warning at all, and the team put it down to a faulty gauge. By midday the engineer had lowered a probe into the shaft and found nothing down there but a plug of gravel. Early in the afternoon two workmen cleared the passage by hand, carefully, stone after stone. The flow came back all at once. Water shot up over the rim of the basin, then eased into a steady trickle. In the evening we took our readings and set them against the week's curves. It comes down to one line. The rock up here breaks apart under pressure, and it will block the shaft again every season. A metal grille is going in upstream. I shall be home again as soon as the report has been signed.

units: water works into hollows too fine to be seen
freezing increases the space the water takes up
that increase in volume widens the crack
the crack stays open once mild weather returns
mineral deposits and roots settle into the opening
the pressure of the plants completes the break

those particles help to build a soil
the bare slope and the grassland below share the same origin
moving air carries the finest fragments down to the low country
text: What becomes of a stone once the water has settled itself in its veins? It learns patience for a long while, and then it gives way. The water works into pores so fine that no eye can pick them out. Cold comes, the water stiffens and pushes outward, and the crack widens by a hair. The thaw returns, the water drains away, and the opening stays. What follows? A dust of minerals gathers there, roots take hold, and the pressure of growing things finishes the work. Should we say that the rock dies? No, it scatters. Every fragment travels down the slope, grinds against its own kind, and ends up as grains of matter that feed a soil in the making. Moving air carries the lightest of them off towards the low country. The bare slope above and the grassland below are one and the same matter, parted by a long fall.

units: the filtering system was clogging far faster than expected
the readings showed mostly clay particles
these particles turn sticky as soon as they meet damp
the clogging happens in the lower part of the system
the supervisor put forward a coarse screen at the inlet
she also put forward a settling tank ahead of the system
the technician feared a loss of flow at peak demand
two tanks used in turn solved the flow problem
the time between two clogging events has been greatly lengthened
text: The technician down at the site told the supervisor that the inlet filter was now clogging up in a fortnight rather than in six weeks. She asked him whether the load of particles had gone up. He said the analyses pointed mainly to fine clay, which turns sticky the moment it meets damp and seals the mesh from below. The supervisor put forward a coarse screen on the raw water, wide bars, ahead of everything else, and a settling tank to hold the water before it reaches the filter. The technician objected that a tank would drag the flow down at peak demand. She suggested two tanks running side by side, with a switch from one to the other. The trial was left to run for a whole season. The filter now holds for eight weeks, and the crew clean the tanks out, which costs less than replacing mesh.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the study of rock once rested on the senses of the researcher
the observer weighed the stone, tested its hardness and listened to the sound of the blow
descriptions depended on the memory of the person observing
two researchers far apart gave different names to the same material
cutting the rock into a transparent slice changed the discipline
this technique makes the crystals and their arrangement visible
the old approach was quick but confused materials that looked alike
the new approach calls for equipment and patience
the two ways of working are still used together in the field
text: Before optical instruments grew fine enough to be trusted, the study of rock rested on the hand and the eye. An observer weighed a block in the palm, scratched it with a fingernail, listened to the sound it made when struck. A description was worth no more than the memory behind it, and two scholars working far apart would file the same stone under different names. The thin section overturned all of that. Cut the rock down until light passes through it and the crystals themselves come into view, their edges and their arrangement, so that matter can be named without being handled. The older method judged the surface, the newer one questions the structure. One was quick and confused stones that felt alike. The other calls for a workshop, patience and a steady flow of cutting water. They still work together, since on the slope the hand picks what the blade will confirm.

units: three kinds of soil share the same slope
the soil in which sand dominates lets water away very quickly
its grains do not stick together between the fingers
clay soil holds water and turns sticky in the rain
as it dries clay hardens and cracks
the middle soil keeps the useful moisture and lets the surplus away

that layer feeds the vegetation
a shaping test done by hand shows which kind dominates
text: Three kinds of soil share one and the same slope, and the hand alone can tell them apart. Sandy soil lets the water slip straight through it. It is open and light, and the grains roll between the fingers without ever sticking together. Clay does the opposite. It holds on to water, turns greasy in the rain, then hardens as it dries until it cracks into plates. Loam sits somewhere between the two. It keeps back enough moisture for the roots and sends the surplus on downhill. Above these three lies a dark surface layer, thick with the remains of plants, which feeds everything that grows. A gardener checks what he is working with by rolling a damp pellet of it round in his palm. It falls apart into dust where sand rules, and rolls out into a smooth thread where clay has the upper hand.

units: the group set off before daybreak to watch a spring that flows in fits

the guide was recording the gap between two occurrences
text: We set off before daybreak to see the spring that empties itself in fits, and I moaned all the way there, because the cold had already got into my fingers. Our guide, a retired stockman, walked us the best part of an hour along a greasy track. When we arrived there was nothing to look at. A steaming hole, a lukewarm puddle, two birds that could not have cared less. He told us to stand still and say nothing. After a while a deep rumble came up through the ground, the puddle drained in a moment, and the water shot higher than the trees, in a warm cloud that soaked us to the socks. It was over quickly, and the quiet came back as though nothing had happened. Our guide was busy noting the gap between one waking and the next. We walked off laughing, wet, delighted, and I stopped moaning.

units: the sample is taken at the depth where the roots grow
the surface layer is set aside because it holds debris
the sample dries away from heat so that its structure is kept

the colour is noted both wet and dry
text: Take your handful of soil at the depth where the roots are, never from the top, because the upper layer is full of debris and would throw the reading out. Spread the sample on paper and let it dry in the shade, since strong heat bursts the crumbs apart and alters the texture. Sieve the dry material to take out the gravel, or its weight will crush the fine fraction in your calculation. Tip whatever is left into a jar of clear water, shake it well, then leave it alone to settle. The heavy grains drop first, the fine ones after, and the bands can be read through the glass. Measure the depth of each band from the bottom upwards, because the order of deposit tells you what the soil is made of. Note the colour down last of all, wet and then dry, since it changes altogether as the moisture goes.

text: Along the low bank the water has eaten the slope back to the roots of the shrubs, and the path that once followed the river is dropping away in whole sections. The people who live there put it plainly: every time the river rises, the bank retreats a pace. The ground is loose here, sand mixed with silt, and the current lifts it without effort as it gathers speed round the bend, carrying the loosened material away downstream. The team responsible for the catchment ruled out a concrete wall, costly and brutal, which would only have thrown the force of the water at the far bank. They chose instead to replant the slope with shrubs that root sideways, to lay bundles of branches at the foot of it, and to dig a hollow upstream to slow the water. One season was enough to hold the toe. The path will be moved uphill, out of reach.
